      {"@context":"http://schema.org","@graph":[{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Hawke's Bay Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hawkes-bay-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-07-30T23:14:15.739Z","headline":"A day in the life with Ranger Alan","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_a-day-in-the-life-with-ranger-alan-activity-7488733732435103745-AE3_","text":"For Al, a good day at work is one spent out in the field, not behind a desk.\n\nAs a Ranger, his days can involve everything from checking trails and river access points to helping keep drainage systems flowing and supporting flood response efforts when needed.\n\nToday is World Ranger Day, and we thought, what better way to recognise the efforts of the man who often operates behind the scenes, than to twist his arm into being on camera and telling us all about his mahi 😉  \n\nCheers to the rangers out there doing their thing for our communities and the environment. Appreciate you 🌟","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_a-day-in-the-life-with-ranger-alan-activity-7488733732435103745-AE3_"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Hawke's Bay Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hawkes-bay-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-07-29T00:25:36.393Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_a-major-milestone-for-p%C4%81k%C5%8Dwhai-and-hawke-activity-7488026911072391168-g778","text":"A major milestone for Pākōwhai and Hawke’s Bay’s flood resilience programme 🌟\n\nSeventy-three Pākōwhai properties have now had their Category 2C classifications removed, taking the affected area out of the Government’s Future of Severely Affected Land framework.\n\nThe milestone reflects significant progress on Hawke’s Bay Regional Council’s $50 million Pākōwhai Flood Resilience Project – the largest flood resilience project of its kind in Hastings District.\n\nDesigned to provide a higher level of flood protection for the former Category 2C area, the project will help support long-term community resilience and confidence following Cyclone Gabrielle.\n\n🚧 Key works include: \n• 8.5km of stopbanks and sheet pile flood walls\n • A 500m stream realignment behind Pākōwhai War Memorial Hall\n • A 230m spillway designed to safely manage floodwater during larger events\n\nHBRC Chair Sophie Siers says the milestone represents much more than infrastructure progress. \"Every property removed from Category 2C represents more than a change in status. It represents greater certainty for families, renewed confidence for communities and another step towards a more resilient Hawke's Bay.\"\n\nDeputy Chair Jerf Van Beek says the decision provides reassurance for the future of the community. \"It shows Pākōwhai remains a place where people can put down roots, invest in their homes, and look ahead with confidence.\"\n\n👷 Construction is being delivered by Hick Bros Civil Construction Ltd and forms part of Hawke’s Bay’s wider $256.5 million flood resilience programme. \n\nThe programme is funded through a partnership between Central Government and Hawke’s Bay Regional Council, with 75 per cent funded through National Infrastructure Funding and Financing and 25 per cent by HBRC.\n\nThank you to our funding partners, delivery partners and the Pākōwhai community for their ongoing support as this work continues.\n\nRead more: https://lnkd.in/e3BZ_nxQ","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_a-major-milestone-for-p%C4%81k%C5%8Dwhai-and-hawke-activity-7488026911072391168-g778"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Hawke's Bay Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hawkes-bay-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-07-20T02:30:04.141Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_making-complex-environmental-data-more-accessible-activity-7484796742283153408-CymU","text":"Making complex environmental data more accessible to the public was one of the key recommendations from the Independent Flood Review following Cyclone Gabrielle. \n\nThis has since shaped a significant piece of work for our team. The updated flood dashboard on our Extreme Weather Hub brings together rainfall and river level monitoring data from across the region into a single interface, designed to support early awareness of changing river conditions and potential flood risk. \n\nThis month, the heavy rain event gave us an early read on how the updated interface is performing in a real-world scenario. More than 800 people used the hub during the event, and the flood dashboard section received over 6,700 views across the long weekend. These are useful signals as we continue to refine the tool. \n\nFlood data is inherently complex. A lot of the design thinking has gone into surfacing the most relevant information clearly, without oversimplifying what the data actually shows. It's an evolving piece of work, and community feedback will keep shaping where it goes next. \n\nExplore the dashboard: https://lnkd.in/e8JY4Jd9","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_making-complex-environmental-data-more-accessible-activity-7484796742283153408-CymU"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Hawke's Bay Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hawkes-bay-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-07-02T03:29:44.247Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_a-hard-won-step-forward-for-p%C5%8Drangahau-75-activity-7478288776751030272-vJmp","text":"A hard-won step forward for Pōrangahau: 75 homes previously classed as Category 2C following Cyclone Gabrielle no longer carry a post-Gabrielle flood risk category under the Government’s Future of Severely Affected Land (FOSAL) framework. \n \nHBRC Chair Sophie Siers says the decision gives the Pōrangahau community something it has waited three years for: a clearer path forward. \n \n“This is so much more than just a technical change,” she says. “For the people who have been living with Category 2C beside their address, it is a letter that says: the ground is firmer now, and you can plan for a future here in Pōrangahau.” \n \nThat future is now taking shape in steel, soil and precise engineering along the riverbank – the first engineered flood protection for a town that has flooded many times. \n \nAlong the northern side of the river, phase one of the $14.6 million Pōrangahau Flood Resilience Project is being built in sections: 1.7 kilometres of stopbanks and sheet pile flood walls, with Galbraith Earthmovers shaping the stopbanks and Lattey Group Ltd driving in the sheet pile walls. \n \nThe Pōrangahau project is funded 72 per cent by Central Government – with that contribution managed by National Infrastructure Funding and Financing (NIFF) through the Government’s Cyclone Recovery Fund – and 28 per cent by the Hawke’s Bay extended whānau through HBRC. \n \nFor HBRC Councillor Thompson Hokianga, the decision lands close to home. \n \n“Pōrangahau is a place that raised me, a landscape I know intimately, and a community I am accountable to, not only as an elected councillor but through whakapapa,” he says. \n \n“So to have that category lifted for these homes is huge. It helps put that future back on solid ground – recorded in writing and made visible on the whenua through the stopbanks and flood walls.” \n \nThe next phase of the Pōrangahau mahi turns to the south side of the river, where properties remain in Category 2C while options analysis and design continue. \n \nAs the next phase begins, Pōrangahau joins Havelock North, Waiohiki, Whirinaki and Ōhiti Road | Ōmāhu as the fifth of Hawke’s Bay’s seven major flood resilience projects to reach this land-category milestone – part of a wider $256.5 million programme to strengthen flood protection across the region. \n \n👉 Read more here: https://lnkd.in/ekDjYy4y","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_a-hard-won-step-forward-for-p%C5%8Drangahau-75-activity-7478288776751030272-vJmp"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Hawke's Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hawkes-bay-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-06-29T03:28:16.548Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_today-our-ce-nic-peet-and-tranzit-group-activity-7477201245347225601-EjLl","text":"Today, our CE Nic Peet and Tranzit Group Managing Director Paul Snelgrove signed a new nine-year contract that will bring an all-electric urban bus fleet to Napier and Hastings from 1 August 2027.\n\nThe new zero-emission buses will help reduce the carbon footprint of our urban public transport network, while supporting a more comfortable passenger experience with wider aisles, a light and airy design, next-stop audio and visual announcements, and CCTV inside and outside buses.\n\nIn a boost for Hawke’s Bay, the charging infrastructure will be supplied by Kwetta, a Napier-based technology company, directly supporting our local economy.\n\nThis contract further supports our wider public transport and climate goals, including our strategic priority of responding to a changing climate. We’ll now work with Tranzit Group on their detailed mobilisation programme, including fleet procurement, depot and charging arrangements, staff readiness, operational systems and customer communications.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_today-our-ce-nic-peet-and-tranzit-group-activity-7477201245347225601-EjLl"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Hawke's Bay Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hawkes-bay-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-06-24T01:15:13.753Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_behold-the-1919-rural-efficiency-guide-activity-7475355823725158400-NTix","text":"Behold the 1919 Rural Efficiency Guide 📖\n\nA VERY comprehensive 1,600 pages covering everything from soil management and farming engineering to somewhat dated (and potentially questionable) medical advice and even a few beauty tips 💅\n\nWarwick, our Principal Land Management Advisor, brought his ‘wee book’ along to our Facebook Live session last night... and we almost had to put some extra support beams under the table.\n\nJoined by Councillor Di Roadley and Councillor Tony Kuklinski, the panel discussed one of Councils priority focus areas: Land and Water Health. This particular session focused on soil conservation; why keeping soil on the hills is critical for our economy, environment, and communities; how catchment partnerships are making a difference; and what it means for landowners, communities, and the future of the region.\n\nWarwick commented that his beloved Rural Efficiency Guide was written during a time when farmers in the United States were walking off their land.\n\n‘After just a few generations of farming, soils had become so depleted and degraded that they were no longer productive.’ He noted that this was essentially the beginning of the soil conservation movement. 'A lot of those techniques, and principals we inherited in New Zealand as part of our soil conservation journey.'\n\n\nYou can check out the full Facebook Live here: \nhttps://lnkd.in/eWWzGTFq for more on soil conservation and it's impacts on Land and Water Health. \n","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_behold-the-1919-rural-efficiency-guide-activity-7475355823725158400-NTix"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Hawke's Bay Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hawkes-bay-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-06-14T22:27:15.213Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_were-hiring-join-our-civil-defence-emergency-activity-7472052060469837824-4bmi","text":"🚨 We’re hiring! Join our Civil Defence Emergency Management team 🚨\n\nIf you’re looking for a career where your work genuinely makes a difference for people, whānau and our communities here in Hawke's Bay, then this is your moment.\n\nOur Civil Defence Emergency Management (CDEM) team is growing, and we’re looking for passionate, purpose‑driven professionals to help shape the future of emergency reduction, readiness, response, and recovery in our region.\n\nWe are looking for a Senior Advisor, Emergency Management - Public Information and Education. \n\nSomeone with a collaborative, team-focused approach who can build strong relationships with communications staff across other organisations to ensure consistent and comprehensive messaging is delivered to the public. You will bring a sound understanding of public information and communication practice within an emergency management or wider public sector context, along with knowledge of nationally consistent messaging, guidance, and good practice relevant to civil defence emergency management. You will stay calm and clear-headed under pressure, which is essential when leading public communications during a response.\n\n💛 Why join us?\nBecause what we do matters. You’ll be part of a team committed to protecting communities, supporting cultural partnerships, leading meaningful change, and ensuring we can face challenges together.\n\nIf you’re ready to use your skills for good and grow in a role with real purpose, we’d love to hear from you.\n\n👉 Check out the role and apply here: Senior Advisor, Emergency Management - Public Information and Education Job in Hastings Central, Hawkes Bay - SEEK","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_were-hiring-join-our-civil-defence-emergency-activity-7472052060469837824-4bmi"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Hawke's Bay Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hawkes-bay-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-06-08T04:30:04.300Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_new-wave-buoy-deployed-off-wairoa-we-deployed-activity-7469606651575300096-LQfz","text":"New wave buoy deployed off Wairoa\n \nWe deployed a new wave buoy about 2.6 km offshore from the Wairoa River mouth on 4 June so we can better understand what’s happening offshore.\n\nThe buoy measures wave statistics (height, direction, etc) and wind speed, then sends that information back to help us:\n• Understand when conditions are more likely to cause the river mouth to close\n• Improve our wave forecasts\n• Support Harbourmaster work to help keep people safe on the water\n• Learn more about how sea spray can affect local air quality\n \nThe deployment was marked with a karakia supported by Tātau Tātau o Te Wairoa.\n\nOur team also cleaned and checked the buoy near the Esk River mouth on the same day. The team will regularly inspect both buoys and carry out any maintenance needed every 3- 4 months.","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_new-wave-buoy-deployed-off-wairoa-we-deployed-activity-7469606651575300096-LQfz"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"DiscussionForumPosting","author":{"@type":"Organization","name":"Hawke's Bay Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hawkes-bay-regional-council"},"datePublished":"2026-06-04T02:28:11.411Z","mainEntityOfPage":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_today-marks-an-important-milestone-for-hawke-activity-7468126427637448704-yZNX","text":"Today marks an important milestone for Hawke’s Bay, with the signing of the Lake Whatumā Accord – a shared commitment to protect and restore one of the region’s most significant wetland taonga.\n\nTogether with Te Rongo o Whatumā, the Department of Conservation, and Central Hawke’s Bay District Council, Hawke’s Bay Regional Council is proud to be part of a collective effort that formalises decades of whakaaro, wānanga and hands-on mahi at the lake. The Accord sets the foundation for a coordinated approach to restoration, aligning planning, funding, delivery and monitoring over the long term.\n\nLake Whatumā is one of the few remaining wetlands of its kind in Hawke’s Bay, and its protection carries deep environmental, cultural and research value for our region and the wider motu. The Accord supports an ambitious 50-year plan to restore the lake and surrounding wetlands, strengthen biodiversity, and ensure its mauri is protected for future generations.\n\nMost importantly, this kaupapa reflects what can be achieved when iwi, councils and central government agencies come together with a shared purpose. By working in partnership, we are building not just a healthier lake, but a lasting legacy for Hawke’s Bay.\n\nPhoto (L-R) Welcome hongi between Central Hawke's Bay District Mayor Will Foley and To Rongo o Whatumā Chairperson Dr Roger Maaka\n\nGroup photo of signatories: Pictured (L to R)\nHawke’s Bay Regional Council Councillor Thomson Hokianga, Department of Conservation Hawke’s Bay Operations Manager Grant Bennett, Central Hawke’s Bay Mayor Will Foley, Hawke’s Bay Regional Council Councillor Tony Kuklinski, Te Rongo o Whatumā Chairperson Dr Roger Maaka","url":"https://www.linkedin.com/posts/hawkes-bay-regional-council_today-marks-an-important-milestone-for-hawke-activity-7468126427637448704-yZNX"},{"@context":"http://schema.org","@type":"Organization","name":"Hawke's Bay Regional Council","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hawkes-bay-regional-council","address":{"type":"PostalAddress","streetAddress":"159 Dalton St","addressLocality":"Napier","addressRegion":"Hawke's Bay","postalCode":"4110","addressCountry":"NZ"},"description":"Our Mission Statement - Enhancing Our Environment Together | Te Whakapakari Tahi I Tō Tātau Taiao\n\nOur Vision:  We want \nA healthy environment, a vibrant community and a prosperous economy.\n\nOur Focus: We prioritise\nWater quality, safety and certainty\nSmart, sustainable land use\nHealthy and functioning biodiversity\nSustainable services and infrastructure.\n\nOur Values:  We believe in\nPartnerships and collaboration\nAccountability\nTransparency\nExcellence.","numberOfEmployees":{"value":325,"@type":"QuantitativeValue"},"logo":{"contentUrl":"https://media.licdn.com/dms/image/v2/D560BAQHSy5KUcYHlUw/company-logo_200_200/B56ZqZcx.eHQAI-/0/1763511050622/hawkes_bay_regional_council_logo?e=2147483647&v=beta&t=6Fn3U2FiHxLN30fPXDHn4AX_GpEuuj6W5-V00poWES0","description":"Hawke's Bay Regional Council","@type":"ImageObject"},"slogan":"Enhancing the environment together 🌱\nHawke's Bay, New Zealand","sameAs":"hbrc.govt.nz"}]}

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">A major milestone for Pākōwhai and Hawke’s Bay’s flood resilience programme 🌟

Seventy-three Pākōwhai properties have now had their Category 2C classifications removed, taking the affected area out of the Government’s Future of Severely Affected Land framework.

The milestone reflects significant progress on Hawke’s Bay Regional Council’s $50 million Pākōwhai Flood Resilience Project – the largest flood resilience project of its kind in Hastings District.

Designed to provide a higher level of flood protection for the former Category 2C area, the project will help support long-term community resilience and confidence following Cyclone Gabrielle.

🚧 Key works include: 
• 8.5km of stopbanks and sheet pile flood walls
 • A 500m stream realignment behind Pākōwhai War Memorial Hall
 • A 230m spillway designed to safely manage floodwater during larger events

HBRC Chair <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/sophie-siers-01796b221?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Sophie Siers</a> says the milestone represents much more than infrastructure progress. "Every property removed from Category 2C represents more than a change in status. It represents greater certainty for families, renewed confidence for communities and another step towards a more resilient Hawke's Bay."

Deputy Chair <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/jerf-van-beek-a018b018?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Jerf Van Beek</a> says the decision provides reassurance for the future of the community. "It shows Pākōwhai remains a place where people can put down roots, invest in their homes, and look ahead with confidence."

👷 Construction is being delivered by <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/hick-bros?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Hick Bros Civil Construction Ltd</a> and forms part of Hawke’s Bay’s wider $256.5 million flood resilience programme. 

The programme is funded through a partnership between Central Government and Hawke’s Bay Regional Council, with 75 per cent funded through <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/nationalinfrastructure?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>National Infrastructure Funding and Financing</a> and 25 per cent by HBRC.

Thank you to our funding partners, delivery partners and the Pākōwhai community for their ongoing support as this work continues.

Read more: <a class="link" href="https://lnkd.in/e3BZ_nxQ?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://lnkd.in/e3BZ_nxQ</a></p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Making complex environmental data more accessible to the public was one of the key recommendations from the Independent Flood Review following Cyclone Gabrielle. 

This has since shaped a significant piece of work for our team. The updated flood dashboard on our Extreme Weather Hub brings together rainfall and river level monitoring data from across the region into a single interface, designed to support early awareness of changing river conditions and potential flood risk. 

This month, the heavy rain event gave us an early read on how the updated interface is performing in a real-world scenario. More than 800 people used the hub during the event, and the flood dashboard section received over 6,700 views across the long weekend. These are useful signals as we continue to refine the tool. 

Flood data is inherently complex. A lot of the design thinking has gone into surfacing the most relevant information clearly, without oversimplifying what the data actually shows. It's an evolving piece of work, and community feedback will keep shaping where it goes next.

  <div class="attributed-text-segment-list__container relative mt-1 mb-1.5 babybear:mt-0 babybear:mb-0.5">
    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">A hard-won step forward for Pōrangahau: 75 homes previously classed as Category 2C following Cyclone Gabrielle no longer carry a post-Gabrielle flood risk category under the Government’s Future of Severely Affected Land (FOSAL) framework. 
 
HBRC Chair <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/sophie-siers-01796b221?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Sophie Siers</a> says the decision gives the Pōrangahau community something it has waited three years for: a clearer path forward. 
 
“This is so much more than just a technical change,” she says. “For the people who have been living with Category 2C beside their address, it is a letter that says: the ground is firmer now, and you can plan for a future here in Pōrangahau.” 
 
That future is now taking shape in steel, soil and precise engineering along the riverbank – the first engineered flood protection for a town that has flooded many times. 
 
Along the northern side of the river, phase one of the $14.6 million Pōrangahau Flood Resilience Project is being built in sections: 1.7 kilometres of stopbanks and sheet pile flood walls, with Galbraith Earthmovers shaping the stopbanks and <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/lattey-group?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Lattey Group Ltd</a> driving in the sheet pile walls. 
 
The Pōrangahau project is funded 72 per cent by Central Government – with that contribution managed by <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/nationalinfrastructure?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>National Infrastructure Funding and Financing</a> (NIFF) through the Government’s Cyclone Recovery Fund – and 28 per cent by the Hawke’s Bay extended whānau through HBRC. 
 
For HBRC Councillor <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/in/thompson-hokianga-aa876970?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Thompson Hokianga</a>, the decision lands close to home. 
 
“Pōrangahau is a place that raised me, a landscape I know intimately, and a community I am accountable to, not only as an elected councillor but through whakapapa,” he says. 
 
“So to have that category lifted for these homes is huge. It helps put that future back on solid ground – recorded in writing and made visible on the whenua through the stopbanks and flood walls.” 
 
The next phase of the Pōrangahau mahi turns to the south side of the river, where properties remain in Category 2C while options analysis and design continue. 
 
As the next phase begins, Pōrangahau joins Havelock North, Waiohiki, Whirinaki and Ōhiti Road | Ōmāhu as the fifth of Hawke’s Bay’s seven major flood resilience projects to reach this land-category milestone – part of a wider $256.5 million programme to strengthen flood protection across the region. 
 
👉 Read more here: <a class="link" href="https://lnkd.in/ekDjYy4y?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" rel="nofollow" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>https://lnkd.in/ekDjYy4y</a></p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Behold the 1919 Rural Efficiency Guide 📖

A VERY comprehensive 1,600 pages covering everything from soil management and farming engineering to somewhat dated (and potentially questionable) medical advice and even a few beauty tips 💅

Warwick, our Principal Land Management Advisor, brought his ‘wee book’ along to our Facebook Live session last night... and we almost had to put some extra support beams under the table.

Joined by Councillor Di Roadley and Councillor Tony Kuklinski, the panel discussed one of Councils priority focus areas: Land and Water Health. This particular session focused on soil conservation; why keeping soil on the hills is critical for our economy, environment, and communities; how catchment partnerships are making a difference; and what it means for landowners, communities, and the future of the region.

Warwick commented that his beloved Rural Efficiency Guide was written during a time when farmers in the United States were walking off their land.

‘After just a few generations of farming, soils had become so depleted and degraded that they were no longer productive.’ He noted that this was essentially the beginning of the soil conservation movement. 'A lot of those techniques, and principals we inherited in New Zealand as part of our soil conservation journey.'


You can check out the full Facebook Live here:

</p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">New wave buoy deployed off Wairoa
 
We deployed a new wave buoy about 2.6 km offshore from the Wairoa River mouth on 4 June so we can better understand what’s happening offshore.

The buoy measures wave statistics (height, direction, etc) and wind speed, then sends that information back to help us:
• Understand when conditions are more likely to cause the river mouth to close
• Improve our wave forecasts
• Support Harbourmaster work to help keep people safe on the water
• Learn more about how sea spray can affect local air quality
 
The deployment was marked with a karakia supported by <a class="link" href="https://nz.linkedin.com/company/t%C4%81tau-t%C4%81tau-o-te-wairoa?trk=organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" target="_self" data-tracking-control-name="organization_guest_main-feed-card-text" data-tracking-will-navigate>Tātau Tātau o Te Wairoa</a>.

Our team also cleaned and checked the buoy near the Esk River mouth on the same day. The team will regularly inspect both buoys and carry out any maintenance needed every 3- 4 months.</p>

    <p class="attributed-text-segment-list__content text-color-text !text-sm whitespace-pre-wrap break-words
        " dir="ltr" data-test-id="main-feed-activity-card__commentary">Today marks an important milestone for Hawke’s Bay, with the signing of the Lake Whatumā Accord – a shared commitment to protect and restore one of the region’s most significant wetland taonga.

Together with Te Rongo o Whatumā, the Department of Conservation, and Central Hawke’s Bay District Council, Hawke’s Bay Regional Council is proud to be part of a collective effort that formalises decades of whakaaro, wānanga and hands-on mahi at the lake. The Accord sets the foundation for a coordinated approach to restoration, aligning planning, funding, delivery and monitoring over the long term.

Lake Whatumā is one of the few remaining wetlands of its kind in Hawke’s Bay, and its protection carries deep environmental, cultural and research value for our region and the wider motu. The Accord supports an ambitious 50-year plan to restore the lake and surrounding wetlands, strengthen biodiversity, and ensure its mauri is protected for future generations.

Most importantly, this kaupapa reflects what can be achieved when iwi, councils and central government agencies come together with a shared purpose. By working in partnership, we are building not just a healthier lake, but a lasting legacy for Hawke’s Bay.
